## Overview

Most ecological cellular automata are stochastic: infection, dispersal and
death happen with probabilities. This vignette covers how random numbers work
in `CellularAutomataCore.jl`, why the same model gives the same answer however
it is run, and how to run and summarise ensembles of replicates with the SciML
ensemble interface.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
using Random
using Statistics
```

## Counter-based random numbers

A rule draws random numbers from its context: `uniform(ctx, k)` is a number in
$[0, 1)$ and `bernoulli(ctx, p, k)` is `true` with probability `p`. The draw is a
pure function of four things, hashed by the Philox4x32-10 generator
[@Salmon2011]:

1. the problem's `seed`,
2. the cell,
3. the time step,
4. the draw number `k`.

Nothing depends on the order in which cells are visited, so the result is the
same on one thread or many, on the CPU or a GPU, with dense or sparse storage.
Different `k` give independent numbers; the same `k` gives the same number, so
a rule should number its independent events `1, 2, …`. (Draw `0` is reserved
for the update schemes.)

```{julia}
ctx = CellContext(nothing, CartesianIndex(3, 4), 10, 42, 2026)
uniform(ctx, 1), uniform(ctx, 1), uniform(ctx, 2)
```

## Directed percolation

The Domany–Kinzel automaton is the simplest model of an epidemic in one
dimension. A cell becomes (or stays) active with probability $p$ if at least one
of its two neighbours was active, and is otherwise inactive. Activity either
dies out or spreads forever, with a sharp transition near $p_c \approx 0.7055$,
the critical point of directed site percolation.

```{julia}
domany_kinzel = LocalRule(Moore(1)) do cell, nbrs, ctx
    any(==(1), nbrs) && bernoulli(ctx, ctx.p.p) ? one(cell) : zero(cell)
end
panels = map((0.62, 0.7055, 0.78)) do p
    sol = solve(CAProblem(domany_kinzel, single_seed(301), 200, (p=p,); seed=3))
    plot(sol; c=:binary, colorbar=false, title="p = $p", xlabel="", ylabel="")
end
plot(panels...; layout=(1, 3), size=(900, 330))
```

The survival probability, the fraction of runs still active after `T` steps,
shows the transition. An `EnsembleProblem` built on a `CAProblem` gives
trajectory `i` the seed `prob.seed + i`, so replicates differ; `output_func`
reduces each run to a number, and `EnsembleThreads()` spreads the replicates
over the threads.

```{julia}
function survival(p; T=150, n=200)
    prob = CAProblem(domany_kinzel, single_seed(401), T, (p=p,))
    ens = EnsembleProblem(prob; output_func=(sol, ctx) -> (any(==(1), final_state(sol)), false))
    sim = solve(ens, Synchronous(), EnsembleThreads(); trajectories=n, save_everystep=false,
                backend=ArrayBackend(threaded=false))
    return mean(sim.u)
end
ps = 0.60:0.02:0.82
plot(ps, survival.(ps); marker=:circle, xlabel="p", ylabel="P(still active at t = 150)",
     legend=false, size=(600, 350))
vline!([0.7055]; linestyle=:dash, color=:grey)
```

## A lattice SIR epidemic

On a square lattice, a susceptible cell is infected by each infectious von
Neumann neighbour independently with probability $\beta$, and an infectious
cell recovers with probability $\gamma$ per step:

```{julia}
sir = LocalRule(VonNeumann(1); states=(:S, :I, :R)) do cell, nbrs, ctx
    if cell == :S
        k = count(==(:I), nbrs)
        return bernoulli(ctx, 1 - (1 - ctx.p.β)^k, 1) ? :I : :S
    elseif cell == :I
        return bernoulli(ctx, ctx.p.γ, 2) ? :R : :I
    end
    return cell
end

u0 = fill(:S, 101, 101)
u0[51, 51] = :I
prob = CAProblem(sir, u0, 200, (β=0.5, γ=0.2); seed=1)
sol = solve(prob; saveat=25)
code(s) = s == :S ? 0 : s == :I ? 1 : 2
plot([plot(Torus(101, 101), code.(sol.u[i]); c=[:lightgrey, :red, :steelblue],
           colorbar=false, title="t = $(sol.t[i])") for i in 2:5]...;
     layout=(1, 4), size=(900, 250))
```

`SavingCallback` records a summary at every step without keeping whole
states; here, the number of infectious cells:

```{julia}
prevalence = SavedValues(Int, Int)
solve(prob; callback=SavingCallback((u, t, integ) -> count(==(:I), u), prevalence),
      save_everystep=false)
plot(prevalence.t, prevalence.saveval; xlabel="t", ylabel="infectious cells", legend=false,
     size=(600, 300))
```

### Final size against transmissibility

The final number of recovered cells is random: small outbreaks die out early,
large ones sweep the lattice. An ensemble for each $\beta$ shows both the mean
and the spread:

```{julia}
function final_sizes(β; n=60)
    p = remake(prob; p=(β=β, γ=0.2), tspan=400)
    ens = EnsembleProblem(p; output_func=(sol, ctx) -> (count(==(:R), final_state(sol)) / length(u0), false))
    return solve(ens, Synchronous(), EnsembleThreads(); trajectories=n, save_everystep=false,
                 backend=ArrayBackend(threaded=false)).u
end
βs = 0.05:0.05:0.6
sizes = final_sizes.(βs)
scatter(repeat(βs; inner=60), reduce(vcat, sizes); alpha=0.25, markersize=3, label="replicates",
        xlabel="β", ylabel="final size (fraction recovered)", size=(650, 380))
plot!(βs, mean.(sizes); lw=2, label="mean")
```

Below $\beta \approx 0.15$ every outbreak stays tiny. From $\beta = 0.2$ most
runs infect most of the lattice, but some always die out after one or two
infections (the replicates at zero), so the mean lies below the bulk of the
replicates. The final size of a major outbreak approaches the whole lattice as
$\beta$ grows.

## Reproducibility

Because every draw is a function of the seed, the cell, the time and `k`:

- the same problem and seed give the same result on every backend and thread
  count;
- an ensemble solved with `seed=...` is reproducible whether it runs serially
  or on threads;
- changing the seed, by `remake(prob; seed=...)`, gives an independent run.

```{julia}
a = solve(prob; backend=ArrayBackend(threaded=false), save_everystep=false)
b = solve(prob; backend=ArrayBackend(threaded=true), save_everystep=false)
c = solve(prob; backend=ReferenceBackend(), save_everystep=false)
d = solve(prob; backend=SparseBackend(:S; tilesize=16), save_everystep=false)
final_state(a) == final_state(b) == final_state(c) == final_state(d)
```

```{julia}
ens = EnsembleProblem(prob)
s1 = solve(ens, Synchronous(), EnsembleThreads(); trajectories=4, seed=7, save_everystep=false)
s2 = solve(ens, Synchronous(), EnsembleSerial(); trajectories=4, seed=7, save_everystep=false)
[final_state(x) for x in s1.u] == [final_state(x) for x in s2.u]
```
